_why: ADR 0114's table. Bakker's 'the evidence did not choose' now reaches the
CLI, and these are the ways that could silently stop being true.
_why_both_files: The rendering test MOCKS the resolver, so it cannot see a parsing
regression -- which is exactly how ADR 0109's first set produced two
confident NOT CAUGHTs. The boundary test drives the real subprocess
through the stub runner. One file proves the CLI renders what it is
handed; the other proves anything hands it over. Neither is sufficient
and the harness said so out loud last time.

mutations.description: the tie is dropped at the boundary (the original defect)
_note: The state the CLI shipped in for the life of the feature: the runner
emits `selectionTie`, `literatureResolver.ts` never reads it, and a
student is handed 21.1 out of a 306-fold spread with nothing saying

mutations.description: the tie is parsed but never rendered
_note: The half-fix: plumbed through the type, carried across the boundary,
and printed by nobody. ADR 0039's defect, and the reason the CLI
tests assert on rendered output rather than on the object.

mutations.description: a one-candidate 'tie' is announced as a tie
_note: Fewer than two candidates is not a tie. `SelectionTie()` with an
empty list is also what an unpopulated field looks like, which is
A warning about nothing is worse than no warning: it trains readers
to skip warnings, which is the one thing this project cannot afford

mutations.description: the alternatives lose their reference ids
_note: A bare count is unactionable -- the reader has to be able to go and
look at the row that was NOT returned. `selection_tie.py` says it:
'a named alternative is checkable; a bare number is not.'

_ran_singly: S1..S4 were each run with `--only`, because the two-file suite costs
~25s and a baseline plus four mutations exceeds the sandbox's per-call
ceiling. The `--only` flag exists for this (ADR 0083): it splits the run
without splitting the record. All four caught.
